MR. LUNDRIGAN-REQUEST FOR CHANGING OF WORD USED BY MEMBER IN REFERRING TO NEWFOUNDLAND JUDGE IN MAY 18 DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a question of privilege which relates to my verbal disability. If Your Honour and the House will bear with me for a moment I should like to ask the House to consider an amendment to Hansard. On May 18 of the present year a statement was attributed to me in the debate on the redistribution of seats in Canada. I was referring to a judge of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland who was in charge of the Newfoundland boundaries commission, and I used the term, "notorious" judge. Then I was reminded by an hon. member that the word should be "noteworthy", and I made the correction as found in Hansard.
I was somewhat surprised when on July 16 I received a two-page reprimand from His Honour, with supporting documentation from other distinguished gentlemen of the court of Newfoundland, asking that I be a little more careful with my language and that I recognize the meaning of a particular word. I replied to the distinguished gentleman on August 8, and I should like to quote one brief paragraph from that letter:
I know my choice of words, although laterly corrected, would prick the sensitivity of one of Newfoundland's elder statesmen and gentlemen. I can assure you that my language choice was purely a form of verbal "subrogation" which is frequently associated with outport Newfoundlanders, especially those of us who speak off the cuff rather than the premeditation of the brain.
I thought, Mr. Speaker, that that would have resolved the problem and would set the record straight. Thus I was a bit surprised today to receive in the mail a letter from His Honour, who has now retired, which says, in essence, that he could not rest if the record were not permanently corrected. Therefore I wonder whether the House would consent to have the permanent record corrected to read "noble" or "noteworthy" judge, or some such word as that, which would convey the respect and honour that should be associated with a man who has now retired from such an eminent position. Perhaps I could also apologize for my language in that respect.
While I am at it, though it was not on the official record may I say I used exactly the same word in 1967 during my first speaking engagement to an eminent body of educators in introducing Sister Nolasco, who is now dean of graduate studies at Carleton University.

subtopic: FISHERIES
FISHERIES
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON FLEET EXPANSION IN ATLANTIC COAST INDUSTRY, SUBSIDIES AND LICENSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, there has been a three-month freeze on subsidies for new fishing vessels on the Atlantic coast. It was introduced in August in order to slow down a boom in fishing vessel construction which was unprecedented. With the continuing depletion of a number of our more important fish stocks, we are in danger of over-capitalizing a fleet which is already large and which should be tailored to future needs rather than expanded on all fronts.

November 14, 1973
Fisheries
During our recent three-month moratorium we have discussed the twin questions of federal subsidies and additional licensing with representatives of the fishermen, the fishing companies and the provincial authorities. While new vessels are needed, especially in the offshore trawler fleet, it is generally agreed that the number of new entrants into the industry should be controlled. More attention should be given to catching species of fish which have not previously been taken in large numbers by Canadians and a determined effort made to take up our international quota for cod in northern areas. Less effort should be directed toward the harvesting of traditional species some of which are over-exploited at the present time.
As a result of these consultations, we have decided to lift the freeze on subsidies. The accent from now on will be on modernization. Replacements and conversions of existing vessels will be encouraged. Grants will also be given for new vessels to be used in areas where the resource is plentiful. The customary 35 per cent subsidy will not be paid, however, in fisheries where it is agreed that we have too much catching capacity. This is true of lobsters, scallops, herring, salmon and snow crab.
A word with respect to licensing, Mr. Speaker. All fishermen presently in the industry will be protected. New entrants will be encouraged as long as they do not add, unnecessarily, to the over-all pressure on fish. To do this, we need to know who are bona fide fishermen and who are not. We need this licensing data in order to upgrade the fishery. We need it in order to develop a sound system of catch insurance as well.
Accordingly and effective immediately: (a) All commercial fishing vessels, traps and other catching units will be registered by the Fisheries and Marine Service; (b) all vessels, skippers and operators will be licensed; (c) only Canadian citizens and landed immigrants will be eligible; (d) all craft, skippers, crews and other operators which have a history in the industry will continue, automatically, to have the right to fish; (e) new entrants will be limited, in the case of lobsters, scallops, salmon, herring and snow crab fisheries to replacements. As hon. members know most of these fleets are already limited in size; (f) new vessel registrations in the groundfish fishery will be encouraged for underexploited species and areas. As for those that are fully exploited the moratorium on new vessel registrations will be continued for a nine-month period. This time is required for further consultations with fishermen, companies and the provinces as to the future of the industry; (g) special committees will be set up in our principal fishing areas in order to advise the government as to the manner in which this program should be administered; and local fishermen and local company representatives will have a voice in the management of the fishery in this way.
Registration of vessels and the issuance of operators' licences will begin early in the new year, and will start with large vessels and the fleets which are already limited in size.
I hope this statement comes across as being optimistic in tone, Mr. Speaker. We have negotiated new and larger quotas in the North Atlantic fishery. Canadians can also

take many species of fish which they have not harvested in the past. So, while we have too many boats chasing too few fish in some areas, we can redirect our efforts and expand our activity in others.
We must increase our over-all capacity and if we do this wisely we will increase the income of our east coast fishermen substantially in the years ahead. The industry agrees with this approach because it is sound from a conservation point of view. It will also increase the average income of our fishermen in eastern Quebec, the Mari-times and Newfoundland.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of the Official Opposition may I say that we listened with considerable interest to the lengthy statement made today by the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis) concerning the government's Atlantic fishing vessel licensing program and subsidies policy.
I wish to thank him for the courtesy he has shown to this side of the House by giving us a copy of his remarks at least an hour before delivering them, a policy which I would commend to other ministers of the government.

subtopic: FISHERIES
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON FLEET EXPANSION IN ATLANTIC COAST INDUSTRY, SUBSIDIES AND LICENSING
speechtext:
When the minister announced the start of a thorough review and assessment of the Atlantic fishing fleet development program on August 13 he indicated that the review would lead to the introduction of new licensing and vessel construction subsidy policies, and at that time he stated that an immediate three-month freeze would be placed on construction subsidies available under the fishing vessel assistance regulations. That type of unilateral action as contained in the minister's statement, along with his statement today, has of course been the hallmark of the present minister. He will go down in history for his acts of confrontation rather than his acts of consultation on the fisheries.
The present government's policies have been dictatorial, coercive, abrasive and contradictory. On the one hand, this minister has asked the fishermen to go out and catch more fish. On the other hand, he has made it extremely difficult for the industry to expand, thereby creating problems for our fishermen, our processors and shore workers who would otherwise gain from increased catches. When I sit in on fishermen's meetings and discuss their problems with them it immediately becomes evident that they are concerned and worried about the regulations emanating from Ottawa and the degree of control presently exercised over their operations and industry by the present Minister of Fisheries and his staff.
The vessel inspection report put out by the minister at the beginning of the 90-day freeze is a classic example of what can happen when he and his staff confront rather than consult the fishermen. The fisheries officers along the coast have valiantly tried to carry out bureaucratic Ottawa's dictates but they have found it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to secure the signature of the captains or owners after inspecting the inshore or offshore fleet. Under this situation I wonder on what grounds the minister has today based his statement concerning the licensing of ships, operators and crews. The captains and
November 14, 1973

owners refuse to sign the forms because they have no confidence in this minister or in this government. This is understandable since, long after the minister announced his freeze on ship construction subsidies due to a lack of funds, the government made vast amounts available on some dubious and questionable make-work projects while at the same time they preferred to spend more than $2 billion on unemployment benefits, some of which would have stimulated the shipbuilding industry in Atlantic Canada.
When the industry is allotted catch quotas through the efforts of government certainly there has to be a partnership between industry and government to plan for the most efficient fishing effort and, undesirable though it may be, licensing may be the only answer. But the average fisherman today, especially the inshore fisherman, seriously questions the quota allotted to him and he asks, for example, why he is prevented from catching herring on Georges Bank next year beyond 25,000 tons while Russia is allocated 342,500 tons. This summer, while the minister was talking about a 200-mile controlled limit on our continental shelf, our fishermen were denied the right to fish for herring in the Bay of Fundy.
In his freeze on construction subsidies we on this side cannot help but wonder why the minister penalized the growth of the Atlantic lobster and the Pacific salmon fleets which are already licensed. Now he wants to further control and manage these fisheries by demanding that the fishermen obtain entry permits before they can go fishing. He has added scallop, herring and snow crab to the list of controlled fisheries and these existing fishermen will still not receive construction subsidies.
We welcome the minister's statement that subsidies at the current level will be provided for replacement vessels, conversion of existing vessels to increase productivity, and for new vessels designed to fish unexploited stocks. However, as the minister is well aware, the quantity of unexploited stocks in the North Atlantic is definitely limited and his moratorium or freeze on new vessel registrations for an additional mine months will definitely be harmful to the over-all expansion of our fishing industry. This action makes a mockery of the minister's statement that our stand at the upcoming Law of the Sea Conference is to give Canadians a larger share of the harvest from fisheries resources off our coast.
Finally-and it was a long statement by the minister- we on this side share the fishermen's concern over the minister's statement of August 13 that vessels already fishing, or for which firm commitments have been made, will be granted licences providing they meet existing regulations. All the special committees representing all the fishing interests, including provincial representation, will not upgrade more than half of the existing fleet to meet the new regulations. In our view, too strict an application of this particular clause could well work a hardship on our existing inshore and offshore fleets. If it is the government's intention to enforce the new regulations strictly before licences are issued, then the government should be prepared to pay an improvement construction grant, in the same manner that assistance is provided shore-based industries, in order to enable the fishermen to
Fisheries
upgrade their boats and equipment in compliance with the new regulations.
Obviously the intent of this new policy is to encourage diversification through multipurpose vessels, but we are concerned about the overlapping authority granted to inshore and offshore licensing committees which is bound to be confusing when applied to multipurpose vessels. We also believe that the new fee structure will restrict young progressive fishermen from entering into new areas of opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I join the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) in thanking the minister for having made available a copy of his statement far enough in advance of delivery for us at least to examine it in a preliminary way. The twin subjects of the vessel construction subsidy and the plans for the licensing of fishermen and fishing vessels constitute the nuts and bolts of the whole fabric of the involvement of the individual fisherman in making a living. Therefore I am sure all hon. members will appreciate the importance of the statement the minister has made today which, as I read it, introduces some rather drastic innovations in past practices on the Atlantic coast of Canada. As I read the statement I find that it introduces in many ways a system parallel to that which fishermen on the Pacific coast have enjoyed, or perhaps I should say endured, for a good many years. In that respect perhaps it does not represent any drastic departure from the over-all policy of the Department of Fisheries.
Only time and a much more extensive analysis than one can make at this point will determine whether or not the minister's proposals are adequate and feasible in the circumstances of the Atlantic coast fishing stocks and our arrangements under ICNAF. They may be the subject of

extended consideration by the fisheries committee in due course.
The principal point on which I would like to comment is the reference in the minister's statement to the fact that consultations were held during the three months freeze with the industry, with fishermen and with provincial governments, and the later reference to the fact that local consultative committees are to be established. In the view of those with some awareness of the outlook of the fishermen this is the key point that should be commented upon in connection with the statement rather than engaging in an attempt to analyse all the details of the specific proposals.
I suggest to the House-and this is in agreement in part with the remarks made by the hon. member for South Shore-that as long as parliament continues to allow a Fisheries Act to stand on the statute books which gives absolute discretion to the minister in the matter of leases and licences to fish, then for just so long will we be engaged in debate on whether consultation has been meaningful or meaningless. The fact is that under the law the minister does not have to consult with his cabinet colleagues, does not have to consult with members of the House, does not have to consult with the fishermen. All too often the fishermen themselves, and some of us in this House, feel that the minister, while going through certain motions, does in fact act in a very dictatorial and at times inscrutable manner when making decisions.
This is the principal question that should be raised at this point. It is certainly the point of view from which Atlantic coast fishermen should examine the new proposals with respect to the licensing of fishermen and boats. I am sure they will do so in relation to the real question of the proper conservation and utilization of the fishing resources of Canada.

speechtext:

What steps has the government prepared to ensure that all Canadians serving with international peacekeeping organizations will have ballots and the right to exercise their votes in the next federal election, including members of the Canadian Armed Forces, Department of External Affairs and those seconded to other agencies?
2.	How many Canadians serving with such international organizations were eligible to vote in the last federal election and how many of these did in fact exercise their franchises?

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FEDERAL ELECTION-VOTING BY CANADIANS SERVING WITH INTERNATIONAL PEACEKEEPING ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
1. The Special Voting Rules (Schedule II to the Canada Elections Act) already contain provisions for the establishing of voting places outside Canada at a federal general election to take the votes of employees of the Public Service of Canada (Public Service electors) residing outside Canada by reason of their departmental duties and the votes of members of the Canadian Forces (Canadian Forces electors) on full-time service. The rules also provide for the taking of the votes of eligible dependants (dependant electors) of the aforementioned electors when residing outside Canada with the elector. The rules require voting places to be established by a head of post or Commanding Officer, as appropriate. No additional or special provisions are required in the Canada Elections Act or the rules to take the votes of Public Service or Canadian Forces electors, and their eligible dependants, serving outside Canada with international peacekeeping organizations.
2. Statistics are not maintained respecting the exact location or precise duties of Canadian Forces or Public Service electors employed outside Canada nor in respect of dependant electors. However, there were approximately 1826 Public Service electors, 8970 Canadian Forces electors and 14,556 dependant electors outside Canada at the last federal election who were eligible to vote under the Special Voting Rules. Since in many cases voting places

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, although it would be appropriate for the Minister of Finance if he were present. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has indicated that the government is prepared to grant increases in the prices of
November 14, 1973

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SUGGESTED ABSORPTION BY GOVERNMENT OF EXPECTED INCREASE IN PRICE OF HOME HEATING OIL PRODUCED FROM IMPORTED CRUDE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government's preference has been to apply the very considerable sums involved from the public treasury in order to make certain, by offshore purchases, that there will be home heating oil available for Canadians this winter. The financial resources have been applied to the priority of making sure of supply rather than reducing the price.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ABSORPTION BY GOVERNMENT OF EXPECTED INCREASE IN PRICE OF HOME HEATING OIL PRODUCED FROM IMPORTED CRUDE
speechtext: In view of the very substantial increase in the revenue the government receives from the 12 per cent sales tax on gasoline and the very substantial increase in revenue the government has already derived from the very significant increases in gasoline prices this year and will derive from anticipated increases, is the government not in a position, as a result of these increased revenues from the sales tax on gasoline, to do what the minister says was done with regard to assuring supplies and also provide the relief I am suggesting with respect to the increased price of home heating oil, which will hit so heavily many Canadians on low incomes?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SUGGESTED ABSORPTION BY GOVERNMENT OF EXPECTED INCREASE IN PRICE OF HOME HEATING OIL PRODUCED FROM IMPORTED CRUDE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am advised that to roll heating oil prices back to their October level would cost $65 million, to roll them back to the November level would cost $42 million, and that the increased revenue from the excise tax on gasoline will yield only $12 million up to the end of March.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ABSORPTION BY GOVERNMENT OF EXPECTED INCREASE IN PRICE OF HOME HEATING OIL PRODUCED FROM IMPORTED CRUDE

That is the question I am asking the minister. Is the government prepared to absorb the further increases for which application has been made rather than allow ordinary Canadians, many of them on very low incomes, to face this disastrous situation?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. I say to him at once that I do not place any blame on him for this but rather on his predecessor. What is the present situation concerning the apparent revolt which took place in Prince Albert penitentiary, and why were the terms of the prisoners accepted? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the morning of November 11 three inmates overpowered three guards in the yard at the Prince Albert Penitentiary and held those guards as hostages. They made four
Oral Question Period
demands, one of which was that two of the men be transferred to the British Columbia penitentiary. The other demands were that no reprisal or action be taken against them and that they be given certain medication. The director of the penitentiary responded to the demand for the transfer of the men to the British Columbia penitentiary but did not accept the request that no action be taken against them. As a matter of fact, criminal action will be taken against them for the offence. Further the doctor at the penitentiary did no see fit to provide them with the medication they requested; he simply said they did not need it. I am advised that the two men in question are still awaiting transfer to the British Columbia penitentiary, and that the delay has been caused by a lack of a proper flight to take them there. Other than that, the penitentiary is in fact back to normal.
To alleviate the overcrowding problem we are presently negotiating with the province of Alberta to take over the Bowden Institute in the constituency of Red Deer. We are also constructing a new medium security institution at Mission, British Columbia, which we hope will further relieve the overcrowding problem.

speechtext:
That it be resolved by the . . . House of Commons:
That it is expedient that the Houses of Parliament do approve the Government's decision that Canadian Forces participate in the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East, and that this House do approve the same.
And that a Message be sent to the Senate informing Their Honours that this House has adopted a resolution approving of the participation of Canadian Forces in the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East, and requesting Their Honours to unite with this House in the approval of the same by filling up the blanks in the resolution with the words "Senate and" . . .

He said: Mr. Speaker, an uneasy ceasefire now prevails in the Middle Eastern battlefield which for 15 days, from October 6 to October 22, and again until October 26, witnessed the most furious and bloody fighting in that beleaguered area in modern times. The most sophisticated and destructive equipment was unleashed in the Sinai desert and the Golan plateau. The biggest tank battles since world war II raged on the ground, while dozens of aircraft were struck down from the skies every day, and in the surrounding waters several naval encounters took place near the harbours of the eastern Mediterranean. Peaceful navigation and trade were interrupted to the point where even some of the government's of that oil rich region were forced to ration gasoline. Casualties mounted rapidly, and even now we are uncertain as to their extent, although the total must be unbearably high, especially in relation to the results achieved.
The mounting fury of the fight was possibly the only reason why it so abruptly ceased. The great powers who were supplying arms in increasing quantity to each side fortunately realized that they were being drawn into a dangerous confrontation, with the Soviet Union talking of unilateral intervention on the scene, while the United States placed its own forces on an increased state of alert. It was at this crucial stage that the United Nations Security Council agreed to the establishment and dispatch of an

November 14, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force emergency force to supervise a ceasefire and separate efforts to prevent a recurrence of the fighting.
Given the circumstances as I have just recalled them, there could be no doubt in anyone's mind that never had an emergency measure of this nature been so evidently and urgently necessary. While Canada did not seek participation in the emergency force, we were determined that once we were invited it would be a success, and I am sure this is a point of view that would be supported by all parties in the House. We were asked at an early stage by the Secretary General of the United Nations to contribute in a vitally important role. Just two and a half hours ago the Secretary General of the United Nations was on the telephone to me urging the importance of Canada's participation and urging our participation in certain of these vital functions upon which the whole of UNEF depends.

speechtext:
After due consideration, the government decided to accept the request and communicated this decision to parliament. In accordance with the practice followed in the past when a Canadian contingent has been contributed to a peacekeeping force, as opposed to the sending of peace observers, we are asking parliament to approve the government's decision. Leaders of all parties represented here indicated, in response to my announcement of October 30, that they supported a Canadian contribution to peacekeeping under the United Nations in the Middle East if it appeared there was a useful role for us to play. Spokesmen for all parties took the same view as I did, that no one could say no to such a request.
The concept of peacekeeping or peace observation forces under the United Nations, which owes so much of its development to a great Canadian, our former prime minister and a member of this House, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson-

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION BY CANADIAN CONTINGENT IN MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION BY CANADIAN CONTINGENT IN MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
-is firmly supported by this government, as it has been by previous Canadian governments of all political stripes. We did not, however, accept the call to join a new UNEF without careful consideration. Experience over the years, some of it rather disappointing, has led us to look for certain criteria that, in our judgment, should be met if a peacekeeping operation is to be effective and if Canadian participation in it is to be worthwhile. We have no illusions that in this imperfect world the criteria for an ideal peacekeeping operation will ever be met in full. These criteria must, however, be constantly reiterated and promoted if peacekeeping is to be made a more effective instrument rather than a source of disillusionment to a world community hungry for peace.
The criteria Canada seeks to apply when considering participation in a peacekeeping operation include certain points of a political nature, as well as others of a more technical kind. A fundamental point is the existence of a threat to international peace and security. There is no doubt of that in this case. Ideally, peacekeeping should be directly linked to agreement on a political settlement among the parties to the conflict. At least there should be reasonable expectations that the parties will negotiate a settlement. The peacekeeping force must be responsible to

a political authority and preferably that authority should be the United Nations. The sponsoring authority should receive reports and have adequate power to supervise the mandate of the force. The parties to the conflict must accept the peacekeeping force and Canadian participation in it must be acceptable to all concerned. Further considerations are that the peacekeeping force must have a clear mandate, including such things as freedom of movement, and that there must be an agreed and equitable method of financing the operation.
Some of these criteria were not met when we participated in the International Commission in Viet Nam, or in Cyprus in 1964, or in the UNEF of 1956. After our departure from Viet Nam, I made it clear that certain features of the operation made it impossible for the commission to operate effectively. One major impediment was the absence of a political authority to which it could report.
The United Nations may not be the only possible sponsoring body, but we have not yet found better auspices under which to work at peacekeeping. It is therefore a matter of satisfaction that in the Middle Eastern situation the emergency force should be put under the authority of the UN. To be precise, it is under the command of the United Nations, vested in the Secretary General, and under the authority of the Security Council.
In 1964, the House debated the dispatch of a Canadian contingent to Cyprus under great pressure of time and in circumstances which did not allow for the application of rigorous conditions. The island was on the brink of civil war with intervention threatened from neighbouring countries, and peacekeeping troops had to be sent as quickly as possible. For nine years, the United Nations force in Cyprus has kept conflict from breaking out and it must therefore be counted, to that extent, as a success. It has not, however, led to a settlement of the underlying problems. The absence of a direct link between a peacekeeping force and a negotiated settlement is a weakness, perhaps an unavoidable one, in the Cyprus situation.
Another weakness of the Cyprus peacekeeping operation is the absence of equitable financial arrangements. This time we are determined that the treatment accorded Canada should be equitable to that accorded to other contributing countries. The Secretary General has stated that his preliminary estimates of the United Nations own direct costs for UNEF, based upon past experience and practice, are $30 million for the six month period authorized by the Security Council. These costs are to be considered expenses of the United Nations organization and are to be borne by the members of the United Nations as apportioned by the General Assembly, presumably in about the same proportions as each country's share in the United Nations annual budget. Canada's share of that budget is currently 3.08 per cent. I might point out to the House that even if we did not participate in this peacekeeping operation we would of course still pay our share of the peacekeeping costs.
It is worth recalling that Canadians have been participating for many years in the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization in the Middle East, and that UNTSO continues to exist and to perform a useful role on
November 14, 1973

the ceasefire lines. Our previous experience in the Middle East in 1956, which was the first major United Nations venture in peacekeeping, is naturally very much in our minds at this time. Sadly, we seem to be back where we were 17 years ago. In fact the request to Canada to participate in the 1973 UNEF is due in great part to the fact that we have special skills and experience, not only in peacekeeping generally but in peacekeeping in the Middle East, and in the role that is now assigned to our contingent. I would remind the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that this was the role that was assigned to us at that particular time.
The original request from the Secretary General for Canadian participation on October 27 was in terms of Canada supplying the logistic component of the force. That role has been assigned to us precisely because of the effective way in which Canada discharged it from 1956 to 1967, and the skills that our troops demonstrated in doing their jobs. Two aspects of our previous experience are relevant to the new task assigned to Canada in the same area. First, the way in which UNEF had to terminate its peacekeeping function in 1967 and evacuate the Middle East gave rise to a great deal of discussion, both at the United Nations and in Canada. From that unhappy episode certain lessons have been drawn.
There is no point in participating in a peacekeeping operation unless our participation is acceptable to all, and especially to the sovereign state upon whose soil the force is to be deployed. I can assure the House that we did not accept this task until the Secretary General had given us formal assurance that the presence of a Canadian contingent would be acceptable to all parties, and especially to Egypt, since UNEF will be deployed on Egyptian territory. In addition, I confirmed the Egyptian agreement personally with the Foreign Minister of Egypt when I met him a few days ago in Washington.
Part of the difficulty encountered with the original UNEF in 1956 was that it did not come under the authority of the Security Council and did not have the unqualified backing of the great powers. Nor was the mandate of the force so clearly set out and accepted by the parties concerned. The first UNEF in the Middle East was a brilliant improvisation that brought the international community back from the edge of disaster but could not ensure peace. This time the superpowers jointly proposed a peacekeeping force, and all members of the Security Council, except China, approved.
The Secretary General in his report to the Security Council on October 26, 1973, set out as essential conditions that the force must have at all times the full confidence and backing of the Security Council, and that it must operate with the full co-operation of the parties concerned. This report was approved by the Security Council and we felt more assured that the 1973 UNEF was to be on a sounder basis than that of 1956. It is on that basis that we acceded to the Secretary General's request of October 27 and accepted our assignment on the force.
Subsequently, an argument developed in the Security Council about having representation in UNEF of various geographical and political groupings. We can understand the desirability of having representation of various geographical areas in a UN force. However, Canada does not
Middle East Peacekeeping Force view its participation in UNEF in terms of political representation but in terms of performing an essential function. When I have been asked from time to time shouldn't there be a representative of the Warsaw Pact as well as a representative of NATO, of which Canada is a member, I have said that we do not consider ourselves as acting in the capacity of representing anyone but the international community as a whole.
In any event, the Security Council decided that the logistic role should be shared between Canada and Poland. I have made it clear that there is no objection on our part to working with Poland, provided a clear and practical division of responsibilities can be worked out. Our concern is with the efficient operation of the logistics component. It is unfortunate that the debate in the Security Council delayed the dispatch of logistical support units by a full week and threw some confusion on the Canadian role in UNEF. Following the Security Council's agreement of November authorizing the Secretary General to consult with potential contributors, including Canada and Poland, our ambassador to the United Nations continued discussions with officials from the UN secretariat and Poland on the organization and composition of the logistics element.
At the same time, at the request of the Secretary General evaluation teams were dispatched to Cairo to assess the requirements on the ground. As a result of these discussions the Secretary General requested, and we agreed, that as the first phase in the deployment of a Canadian contingent Canada would provide a signals unit to provide communications for the force. Poland will be dispatching an engineer unit as the first element in its contribution.
The Secretary General is continuing his discussions with both Canada and Poland to determine the next phase of the logistics deployment, and in particular the allocation of functions between the two countries. In these discussions we have sought to consider in a constructive manner proposals put forward by the Secretary General, while having in mind the need to ensure that Canada will be able to provide a useful and effective contribution to the operation of the force. At the moment the government is giving active consideration to a proposal from the Secretary General that Canada provide an air unit. A request has been made to Poland to provide a field hospital unit. In addition, the Secretary General has made suggestions regarding the division of responsibilities between Canada and Poland with respect to the remaining logistic functions. The discussions have been complex and time-consuming, but I am hopeful that we may be in a position to announce shortly the details of the composition of the remainder of the Canadian contingent.
While these negotiations continue, the advance party of the Canadian signals unit arrived in Cairo on November 10. The deployment of this unit should be completed shortly and will number over 400 persons. This unit is being dispatched according to the schedule determined by the Secretary General. He wanted the advance party of the unit on the ground as soon as possible because of the urgent requirement for an effective communications system within UNEF.

November 14, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force
Another point demonstrated by the history of UNEF from 1956 to 1967 is that a peacekeeping force of this kind should be recognized by all parties as a temporary necessity, to help avoid a renewal of fighting while the parties to the conflict take up the fundamental problem which has led them to fight each other in the first place. It is precisely because the parties involved never made any progress toward a peaceful settlement in the ten years following 1956 that ultimately UNEF had to depart without any other prospect than renewed warfare. With this in mind, I stressed on October 22, that while we warmly welcomed the call for a ceasefire, it was vitally important in our view that the ceasefire should lead quickly to negotiations on the basic problems of the Middle East.
There is now a renewed opportunity for the parties involved to employ the respite that UNEF provides to tackle their basic differences. The principles of a just and lasting settlement have been set out since 1967 in Security Council Resolution 242 but until now no progress has been made in implementing that resolution and no negotiations based on its principles have taken place. Resolution 338 of October 22, 1973 which is the basis for the present ceasefire, also deals with the problem of a peaceful settlement. It calls for an immediate beginning to the implementation of Resolution 242 in all its parts and for the beginning of negotiation between the parties under appropriate auspices.
Mr. Speaker, UNEF is not charged with the basic problems involved in a Middle East settlement. Its tasks are limited to supervising the implementation of the ceasefire, the return of the parties to their October 22 positions and the use of its best efforts to prevent a recurrence of fighting. These will be the tests of UNEF and they will be acid tests. Should the parties to the recent conflict fail to comply with the Security Council resolutions and not allow UNEF to operate effectively, the gleam of hope that the ceasefire and Resolution 338 offer will be threatened with quick extinction. Let us pray that the parties involved will therefore quickly agree to comply with these first steps on the road toward peace.
There is no question that Canadians are desirous of a lasting peace and a lasting settlement in the Middle East and, while it may not be the task of UNEF to promote this settlement, it is still the responsibility of every member of the United Nations to do what it can to help bring about this peace and this settlement. In my statement of October 16 I emphasized that
parties to the conflict would first have to agree on the basis of a settlement and terms of reference for such a force for Canada to accept participation in peacekeeping.
Both the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) stressed that our participation could only be undertaken with the consent of the immediate parties involved, and I have dwelt on our efforts to ensure this. I v'ould add that the consent of the parties must be not only to accept the members of the peacekeeping force but also to facilitate its work by complying with the resolution which gave it birth. By their compliance with the Security Council resolutions, the parties will make our task worth while.

There is encouragement in the fact that for the first time in some 20 years Israeli and Egyptian generals have met and signed an agreement on some urgent problems of the ceasefire situation. The governments of Egypt and of Israel displayed wisdom in accepting these arrangements, and I am sure that I speak for all the House when I say that the United States Secretary of State, Mr. Kissinger, deserves high commendation for the effectiveness of his good offices.

We can only hope that these immediate arrangements will lead to further discussions and further agreement.
As I have said, the framework for peace exists in the resolutions adopted by the Security Council. The problem in our view has never been so much one of interpretation as of implementation of these resolutions. I further indicated in the House last week, in reply to a question, that in our view such provisions of Resolution 242-which we can read in either English or French since we are a bilingual country-as those calling for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from occupied territories and the establishment of secure and recognized boundaries for all states in the region, had to be taken together. Naturally, such matters as the drawing of boundaries may prove to be a long task, but is it beyond imagination to devise means of starting the implementation of the various provisions simultaneously?
The so-called Rogers Plan in 1970 provided for partial implementation of Resolution 242, by a simultaneous reopening of the Suez Canal to navigation and a withdrawal by Israeli forces from the east bank of the canal. While that plan failed, the idea of balance is still a valid one. In fact, the whole basis of Resolution 242 is a balance of obligations and commitments. The problem of Palestinian refugees is one of the items in that balance. The resolution affirms the necessity "for achieving a just settlement of the refugee problem" and this problem should be at least broached simultaneously with the other matters I have mentioned. Canada has not forgotten these refugees. We are the third largest contributor to the United Nations agency which looks after their needs and we have just increased by $550,000 our contribution for the current year.
The main thing now is quickly to get around to negotiating "under appropriate auspices" as Security Council Resolution 338 has it. To us, it would seem that the United Nations offers appropriate auspices. Others have mentioned the great powers, or some of them. We would hope that they would exert their influence to stimulate the parties to begin negotiations. To the Canadian government, any auspices would seem appropriate that provide a means whereby talks can begin on the essential aspects of the problem.
For more than 25 years, the United Nations has played the role of mediator, peacekeeper and truce supervisor in the Middle East. We cannot yet be sure that peace is any closer now than in 1948, 1956 or 1967. Once more, the parties in conflict are calling upon the United Nations to step in and give them time, time that can be used to negotiate for peace or to prepare for war. The Canadian
November 14, 1973

government, in accepting to contribute its part to the UN peace effort, is not taking on this commitment in a spirit of blind optimism. We have had too long an experience in this field, the United Nations has had too long an experience in trying to find a peaceful settlement in the Middle East for anyone to be afflicted with that particular defect. We consider that we have a responsibility to the world community and to all the people of the Middle East to do what we can to give them another chance to achieve a peaceful settlement when the fighting has stopped. That is the purpose of UNEF, and the reason for our participating in it. In putting forward this resolution, therefore, I am asking the House to agree that Canada should do its international duty.

This House is invited not to give advice or contribute to a decision, but to approve a decision of the government. The present government has been unable to learn its lesson during the Viet Nam crisis. And if on October 30-as I recognize the quotation from my previous speech used by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp)-we have, based on the available data, accepted that Canada contribute to the peace effort in the Middle East.
Middle East Peacekeeping Force
Since November 1, the day when the Secretary of State for External Affairs made this House aware of new and apparently sudden problems concerning the Canadian contribution to the United Nations intervention in the Middle East, since that day we have been waiting for a debate that would have allowed Parliament to go beyond what we were asking of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on October 30 and like on March 13, 1964 during the Cyprus conflict under the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, and to participate in the decision before troops are sent on the scene of the cease-fire. But once again, we are sorry to see that the government did not wish it to be so and if we rejoiced last Sunday upon hearing about the agreement concluded between Israel and the UAR, we deplored-and still do-the government's attitude regarding the rights and prerogatives of a minority Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, let it be clear that we are in favour of a just, strong and permanent settlement in the Middle East. Neither do we refuse any more than any other Canadian the sacrifices which must be made in pursuing this ideal of peace and whatever form our contribution takes, we want it to be accomplished with generosity and we know that it will be so. However, in expressing our support for the peace-seeking efforts of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, we must none the less play the role we have as the Official Opposition in Parliament.
I am sure that not a single field of government activity should escape Parliament's criticism, not even that majestic and noble field which is the Department of External Affairs. And that is why, Mr. Speaker, it is our intention today to say clearly to the government what we think of its behaviour during these last weeks and it is our intention to go beyond the narrow setting of an incident to question the government and heckle it, if need be, so that it will give us a definition of an overall policy as concerns Canada's participation in those peace missions.
We have absolutely no doubt as to the experience, efficiency, motivation or fair-mindedness of our Canadian troops among the international peace contingents, but we seriously question-and we make no bones about it-the methods used by this government, its approach in its participation to emergency forces here and there in the world.
After the 1967 eviction in the Middle East and the rather sad experience in 1973 in Viet Nam, it is only legitimate and wise, considering the eagerness and unilateralism of this government, to urge it, as we wish to do, to define its course in that field.

The resolution, Mr. Speaker, which the House is called upon today to approve has both obvious and implicit elements which evoke, I am sure, varying reactions from all members of this House. The suggestion that Canada should respond to a call from the United Nations, and do so in both an energetic and efficient manner, when what is at stake may be the shaky calm which is necessary as a prerequisite to serious negotiations between the Arabs and Israelis, is surely something that few Canadians would care to oppose. The suggestion that the government has the legal right, or the legalistic right, to make a

November 14, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force commitment and then seek parliamentary approval, while objectionable in the context of this minority House, lacks neither precedent nor historical model.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it will come as no surprise if I announce at the beginning of my remarks that we in the New Democratic Party intend to support this motion. However, there are a few additional remarks I feel obliged to make before I take my seat.
I suppose I am fortunate in that on many occasions my sense of frustration at the procedures pursued in this august chamber is balanced by my sense of the ridiculous. Otherwise, the utter futility of many of the pseudo-events here would tip me into a suicidal depression. Here we are engaged in a debate to decide whether or not we should send troops to participate in a Mid-East peacekeeping force after the commitment to do so has been made and when a substantial portion of the troops involved is already on its way.
I realize that the minister had the right to assume, on the basis of statements made in this House by party spokesmen, that there was agreement in principle to undertaking the enterprise. I also realize that, once the difficulties at the United Nations had been sorted out, the government was in good faith obliged to react with all possible speed. I suppose I could take comfort in the fact that today's debate maintains the form if not the substance of the obligation, established by custom but obliga-
Middle East Peacekeeping Force tion none the less, for the government to consult parliament before sending troops abroad on active service, but I do not.
Why could not this House have organized itself to respond more quickly to the situation? We could have discussed the matter Friday afternoon, Friday evening, Saturday, Monday or even yesterday. It would have put us out a bit, but then so are the men going over there and their families being put out a bit, to put it mildly. It is not my intention to sound holier than thou in saying this. I am part of this House and as responsible for its actions as anybody else. But all too often we react more like the denizens of some musty retired gentlemen's club than like people charged with looking after the interests of this nation.
I want to give vent to a bit more spleen on a more peripheral issue before I get down to cases. I think it is unfortunate in the extreme that circumstances conspired to oblige the minister, or to make him feel obliged, to dash off to New York and Washington and back again at a time when Canada's acceptability as a participant in the peacekeeping force was in question. I accept the minister's word that he was requested to do so by the Secretary General of the United Nations. I also accept his word that he was not preaching for a call. Further, I believe that the minister would have preferred to have expressed our willingness to participate and then allow the Security Council to accept or reject us. Instead, he did end up looking as though he was overly anxious to participate.
What forced our country into an undignified posture, I believe, was the childish attitude of the two superpowers who insisted upon injecting further elements of east-west confrontation into the Middle East situation, striking more sparks around what is generally acknowledged to be a powder keg. It is my understanding that the United States objected to the inclusion of a Warsaw pact nation in the force, while the Soviet Union insisted upon a "geographical", for which read "ideological", balance. I think it is about time that the two super-powers stopped playing their silly little games, allowing themselves the luxury of ego trips, and began soberly discharging their responsibilities to the world which their power has imposed upon them.
Their latest little game has succeeded in confirming the opinion of all who were inclined to think that Canada is the American's cat's paw that we are just that. I can support such a minor blow to my pride, but it does not endear either the Soviet Union or the United States to me. But that is a minor consideration and one which can be forgiven. Nevertheless, I think it is important to note that the squabbling and nattering that accompanied the creation of the force should provide solid evidence to those nations that believe in the settlement of disputes through negotiation and through the application of such law as applies, rather than through the use of force majeure, that new efforts should be made immediately to create a standing United Nations force which is provided for in the charter.
To return to the role of the superpowers, I was saying that I could forgive them the fact that they, through their little games, had caused my country some not inconsiderable embarrassment. But what cannot be forgiven is the

November 14, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force two superpowers' total lack of responsibility in their approach to the Middle East following the six day war of 1967. Rather than urging their client states to begin the negotiations which were called for in resolution 242, rather than attempting to clear away some of the considerations which prevented negotiations, they encouraged their respective friends in their intransigence. One could not fault either of the two had they tried and failed. The problem is so complex as to seem to defy solution. But they did not try. On the contrary, they supplied arms to the two sides at an ever-increasing rate, and in so doing made the current outbreak of fighting almost inevitable.
Not only that, during the fighting they engaged in posturing and provocation which ended with the United States going to a Stage 3 alert, an alert which places the nuclear forces of its Strategic Air Command at an advanced state of readiness. Now, that is madness. They should be told so in no uncertain terms and reminded of their responsibility to attempt to secure a lasting peace from this truce, shaky as it is. I do not know how much good such representations would do because neither of the two nations shows much disposition to listen to all we lesser mortals when they have the bit in their teeth, but it is our world too and most of us would like to go on living in it. It is that face which makes my party believe Canada has no choice but to accept the invitation to participate in the peacekeeping force, however uncertain its prospects for success may appear to be, and I am pleased to note that the recent exchanges between Egypt and Israel provide a small ray of hope in an otherwise gloomy picture.
The Middle East situation has within it the potential to be to a third world conflict what the Balkans were to the first. That is not a prediction, Mr. Speaker. I am not that pessimistic, but it is, I think, an acknowledgement of the facts. If our presence, and, that of the other nations involved in UNEF, provides even the slightest prospect for an improvement in the situation then it is in the interest of the world and in our own self-interest that we go. It is also our responsibility because we are part of the world community which gave birth to the current situation, and as such we have an obligation to do what we can to assist in the resolution of the problem.
I would hope that the respite from major fighting which the presence of the peacekeeping force may provide will be utilized by all participants in the dispute, and their not so silent partners, to seek ways and means of effectively pursuing the instructions of the Security Council resolution of October 22. I think the world community must seize the same opportunity to acquaint the belligerents and their allies that the situation cannot be allowed to go on festering, that the dangers to world peace are too great to allow it to do so and that any party to the dispute which seems to be devoting less than 100 per cent effort to achieving a solution will be extremely unpopular, indeed. Too much is at stake.
I am not unaware of the difficulties involved in unravelling the Gordion knot that is Middle East politics. I am not unaware of the emotions, the fears, the hatreds and the sense of resolve of all those engaged. It is very easy for me here in Canada to stand in my place and yell: "Do something", but it still needs to be said. It is our world

too, as I said before. It is our world, but at this moment it is their blood, and I know I speak for everyone here when I express, with all the sincerity I can muster, my sympathy for those who have lost loved ones and to those who have been wounded, and when I express also the hope that this time all will find peace and justice and security: The two million Palestinian refugees who have been denied their homeland, the Israelis who have, after 2,000 years of hope, rebuilt their national state and now must constantly guard against its loss, the Egyptians, the Jordanians and the Syrians who suffer the indignity of seeing foreign troops on their soil.
Like other parties in this House, my party has no pat formula to offer for the resolution of the conflict. I can only say on behalf of my colleagues that we stand ready to support the government on any reasonable steps it takes to discharge Canada's responsibilities as a member of the world community in respect of the Middle East.
In relation to the actual contribution we are making to the peacekeeping force, I would like to suggest to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson), who I understand will be speaking later, that it would be of interest to all of us to learn precisely what numbers are being attached to UNEF, what units they represent, what precise roles they will be fulfilling and what major equipment they will employ. We would also be interested to know if any significant numbers of troops have been withdrawn from our NATO brigade or from our own contingent in Cyprus in order to fulfill our commitments. I have some fear that the effectiveness of our forces remaining in Canada and elsewhere in the world might be compromised because our armed forces are now spread so thin, and so many of those sent to UNEF will of necessity be technical support troops of which we do not have a surplus. That remark was not made by way of suggesting we should not have accepted a role in UNEF but by way of suggesting that the Minister of Defence had better soon undertake an examination of the composition of our forces, and the number of roles assigned to them, in order to decide whether or not the two are compatible.
I think at this point it would be appropriate to say a special word of thanks to our troops in Cyprus, who are currently stretched extremely thin and working exceptionally long hours in order to fill in for the troops of other nations which have been transferred from Cyprus to Egypt. They are doing Canada proud. I hope the minister is concerning himself about arranging for the force to be brought back up to strength.
To our troops now in the Middle East, those now on their way and those soon to be sent, we in the New Democratic Party have every confidence that they will acquit themselves with their customary excellence, in a manner which will bring honour to their country.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize that it is the view of my party that the government has acted entirely correctly in accepting the invitation of the Secretary General of the United Nations to contribute a contingent to UNEF. This responsibility which Canada has undertaken is not, as some would have us believe, a romantic gesture of nobility. It is a sober contribution to a desperate attempt to put an end to the fighting in the Middle East and toward world peace. It is an important

contribution in an attempt to build up an accepted mechanism for dealing with armed conflict. It is an acceptance of our responsibilities as a member of the world community and a concrete expression of our commitment to the concept of collective security under the UN. Our selfinterest, if nothing else, dictates that we take every opportunity proffered which has some prospect of strengthening the UN.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Sunday all Canada celebrated Armistice Day, the anniversary of the signature of the treaty which put an end to the Second World War.
Everyone celebrates Armistice Day. It is a civic holiday, but as soon as it is over, we come back to the House of Commons to talk about another conflict which could even turn into another world war since the United Nations are concerned with it, as are the United States and the USSR in one way or another.
Being a pacific country in North America, Canada must also concern itself with this conflict, either by siding with one of the parties concerned or by remaining neutral as a peacemaking agent.
In fact, a contingent of Canadian soldiers is already in the field; they act as observers and members of the UN forces. We have reached a point where all countries of the world, in addition to administering their own internal affairs, have to complicate their parliamentary and governmental proceedings with the Middle East crisis which seems to us to be the focal point of the attention of every country in the world, in that small countries with only three or four million people put in action the economic and military super powers of the whole world.
In 1948, the United Nations provided a measure of stability to this area by providing Israel with fixed borders, thereby giving rise to the Palestinian refugee problem. These refugees, who then numbered about 1,500,000 sought asylum in the small neighbouring Arab countries. Some of them have dug roots there and started a new life, but a great many are still looking for employment and a suitable occupation. Abandoned, without any sort of known organization or leadership, they are faced with continuing discontent among all these displaced persons, the innocent victims of decisions aimed at giving a land to a people who have been wandering for over 2,000 years and trying to settle in all countries of the world, unable on its own to organize itself.
If Israel now has a population of about three million, mainly thanks to the "importation" of money and citizens from many countries of the world, and following the donation or occupation of territories with the support of Great Britain and of the United Nations, we should not forget that the former residents of those territories, mostly Arabs, have had to leave their dwellings either on their own free will or because they were driven out by new occupants. They were expatriated and dissiminated near the borders either in Jordan, in Lebanon, in Syria or in the UAR. Those who have been able to adapt are living fairly
Middle East Peacekeeping Force well but almost 500,000 are still in refuge camps at the mercy of the charity of the United Nations, of the Arab countries or of other nations.
Most of those refugees are people who were too old to start all over again after such a displacement. The same inconveniences may be found in those mass displacements in the case of forced expropriation in our own country when it comes to expropriate thousands of farmers and other citizens conveniently settled on their lands or in their village; the oldest are those who find it most difficult to start again from scratch.
Obviously those refugees living in the Arab countries or in the neighbourhood of Israel are frustrated and are a source of discord but this indicates at least that Israel should be satisfied with the 1948 boundaries and not repeatedly seek to expand its territory which was not freely given by the natives but forcefully granted by agreements concluded by foreign nations, major countries or the United Nations. Those 500,000 Palestinian refugees alone are a hard problem to settle in the midst of a climate of discord.
It is therefore important that Israel be content with the boundaries granted willingly or not in 1948, leave the neighbouring countries at peace and refrain from any attempt at enlarging their territory so that Arab states not be tempted to push Israelis behind boundaries established in 1948.
In 1967, international diplomacy tried to resolve this problem by introducing Security Council Resolution No. 242 which called for the withdrawal of Israel forces back to their boundaries as established in 1948.
In 1967, the famous Six Day war broke out, the Israelis tried to enlarge their territory at the expense of neighbour Arab countries, a territory that had been occupied by Arabs for more than 2,000 years. As years go by, through diplomatic exchanges or takeovers by mere movements of people, utter confusion still shrouds the boundaries of these small countries where one can see Egypt reach friendly agreements with the USSR or Israel with the United States.
And now these two super powers, at the same time as the United Nations, are trying to effect a settlement between small countries that are unable to reconcile their differences themselves. Therefore, this is a tiny nest of dissent right in the middle of Asia, Africa and Europe that threatens to involve the United States and the Soviet Union. Eventually, this small piece of land, where only about 15 million people are living, might give rise to world war III.
It is really surprising that the situation has come to that point. How come these small countries are strong enough to involve all the great powers of the world? This is a mystery that is difficult to explain. But we find ourselves in this really important situation, and we can no longer close our eyes to it. We have seen quite recently Mr. Kissinger propose that an Israeli-Arab peace conference be held around December 9 or 10 in Geneva, but he stated that even though "peace negotiations are positive, a very serious problem will continue to exist, in particular for Israel, as regards the maintenance of its own security."

November 14, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force
Mr. Kissinger explained that it is always difficult to determine the boundaries of these countries, for they differ from those established at the time of the truce. And he added: "What we must avoid above all is that each and every crisis should become a conflict between super-powers."
Things being what they are, Mr. Speaker, what can Canada do? I think we should participate in the activities of the United Nations, like we already do, and participate in the peacekeeping force and co-operate with such benevolent groups as the Red Cross and help the wounded and the prisoners; we should try to bring about peace and understanding between all parties through peace negotiation, a task we have to accomplish as part of the world community and of the United Nations.
Canada's participation in the peacekeeping force of the United Nations should not aim only at fruitful negotiations between belligerents. It must always strive toward the establishment of lasting peace in Middle East and in all the other parts of the world.
May I add that the basic causes of this endless war between Israel and Arab countries goes back to the formation of the state of Israel in 1948; as it is hardly conceivable that the United Nations contingent will be able to settle this conflict now, after 25 years of struggles, discussions, hate and cultivated ambitions, let us hope that we will at least have contributed to dampen violence until better feelings and intelligent arguments make their pacific work in the settlement of this conflict, which could so easily degenerate into a world conflict.
If the countries concerned cannot reach an agreement it is obvious that Canada cannot claim to act under authority. The UN Security Council is the only one that can serve as an impartial referee with some apparent international authority in the present circumstances. All indications allow us to hope that the United Nations will have before too long a military force capable of ensuring peace across the world in the absence of mere persuasion or balance between the armed forces of different countries.
But there is still a long way to go before we reach that objective and that distance must be crossed not only at the international level but also and specially at the level of citizens and families in every country of the world where they must learn to live with all their neighbours as brothers, friends, human beings.
I would like to say in passing, Mr. Speaker, that it is equally regrettable that we are always faced with faits accomplis when we discuss situations as complex as this one.
I would then ask the government to consult all members of the opposition from now on rather than taking on its own decisions that could have so important consequences.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister responsible for the Canadian armed forces, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the discussion of the resolution that is before the House. At the outset, I wish to confirm and, in fact, to emphasize my personal conviction that the govern-

ment's decision to accept the invitation of the United Nations to participate in a newly formed peacekeeping endeavour in the Middle East is a decision that is consistent with our belief as Canadians in doing all we can to help to bring about peace in the world. It is a decision that is consistent with our history and with our commitment to accept the role of international peacekeeping under the United Nations.
In speaking to the resolution, I would like to divide what I have to say into two parts. I would like to speak about what we are going to do and about why we should do it. In the first part, in speaking in detail about what we are going to do, I hope I may be answering at least in part the questions raised by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland), and when I speak about why we should be there, I hope I will answer the central question raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner).
I would like to begin by emphasizing that in my belief what the Canadian armed forces have been asked to do is to undertake a most vital role, to play a most essential part, in the United Nations Emergency Force. I am certain that all of us realize that no military operation of any kind can be effective without good communications. In fact, no military operation of any kind can even begin to function without being linked by good communications in the field. As I stated in the House last week, all of us, even if we are not military people, should know that much about a military mission.
Therefore, I hope that in this continuing discussion of the resolution we will not hear more about the insignificance or about the unimportance of the role that Canada has been asked to play, because exactly the opposite is the case. It is because of their experience, because of their capability, and because of their training that the Canadian forces have been asked by the United Nations to undertake these important duties-

speechtext: Hear, hear!
