speechtext:
-of providing a communications system for the whole emergency force, a force that is expected to number some 7,000 officers and men.
To meet this United Nations request, we are building a contingent around the 1st Canadian Signals Regiment. Also, as my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), said earlier in the debate, we are still discussing with the United Nations the possibility of sending additional personnel to carry out other duties in the support and logistics field, including the possible provision of a small air transport unit. But I wish now to speak specifically about what we have so far agreed to do, and to answer specifically the questions raised by the hon. member for Selkirk.
The 1st Canadian Signals Regiment, which is stationed in Kingston, will be augmented by administrative personnel and other experienced communications personnel from many of our units across Canada. Altogether, the Canadian Signals Unit and its administrative support personnel, will number 481 officers and men. There will, in fact, be 46 officers and 435 other personnel.
November 14, 1973

Our signals unit will, of course, take its own communications equipment to the Middle East. Most of this equipment, which consists of radios, telephone equipment and a teletype capability, is mobile and is regularly installed and carried inside communications vehicles. For this reason, more than 100 Canadian vehicles will be transported to the Middle East. These are made up approximately of 30 jeeps, 44 three-quarter ton trucks and 32 two and a half ton trucks, most of them, as I have said, containing communications equipment. In addition, there will be some 40 trailers of which 16 are jeep trailers, 17 are three-quarter ton trailers, and 7 are one and a half ton trailers. We are also taking 4 fork lift trucks and one large tow truck.
In addition to this somewhat sophisticated and extremely useful communications equipment, we will be taking other supplies that will enable the Canadian contingent to be totally self sufficient for at least the first 30 days of their stay in the Middle East. To achieve this self-sufficiency in the field, our personnel are taking 30 days rations, field kitchens, a central cooking unit and water purification equipment. They will also have enough tents to enable the whole contingent to live and work under canvas. They will also have with them their own electrical generating units and batteries. Altogether we will be moving some 200 tons of equipment, and that is not including the vehicles.
Our personnel, together with the various items of equipment and supplies that I have just enumerated, will be transported to the Middle East by aircraft from Canada's Air Transport Command. Most of the personnel will be carried in our Boeing 707 aircraft and most of the equipment will be moved in Hercules aircraft. For this airlift we will be using two Boeing 707's and 15 C-130 Hercules aircraft. During the first 10 days we plan in total seven round trips for the Boeings and 41 round trips for the Hercules fleet. The flying time for a Boeing from Trenton to Cairo is 12 hours-that is flying time, not total elapsed time-and 18 hours for a Hercules. Our first flights began on Saturday, November 10 and we expect to have the Canadian contingent in place and operating next Monday, the 19th of this month.
Having outlined in some detail what the Canadian forces are going to do, I now wish to say why I believe the Canadian forces must undertake this important responsibility. In saying why we should participate in this peacekeeping endeavour I will try to answer directly a central question that was placed before this House just a short while ago by the hon. member for Saint Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner). The reason we must answer this call is to me compelling and obvious. We are today sending troops to the Middle East for no less a reason than that under United Nations guidance, in the search for a peaceful world, mankind is in fact struggling to enter a new era.
We all know that throughout recorded history men in uniform have left their homelands for only one purpose. That purpose was to fight. But for the past two decades, and really since the United Nations peacekeeping force went to the Middle East in 1956, a new and nobler role for men in military uniform has been slowly, and painfully, but surely taking shape. Men in uniform now leave their homelands not to fight but to prevent fighting. The fact
Middle East Peacekeeping Force that peacekeeping operations under the United Nations have not been successful everywhere takes nothing away from the nobility of the peacekeeping concept. We realize that it may take 100 years, 200 years, or longer until the peacekeeping forces of the world outnumber the potentially aggressive military forces of the world. But however long it takes, the peacekeeping concept in which Canada has given leadership, and on which Canadians are embarked again today, provides the best, ultimate hope for mankind, the best prospect for finally achieving peace throughout the world.
Because we are only at the dawn of a new era we should not be discouraged by the failures of peacekeeping. We should be grateful for the examples, such as Cyprus, where the peacekeeping concept has worked. Above all, we should keep our sights on the long-term hope for mankind that peacekeeping makes possible.
Now, Mr. Speaker, apart from what some may consider these idealistic reasons for Canada's participation in a peacekeeping role under the United Nations, there is a much more practical reason why we should participate. That reason, simply stated, is that because of the experience and the training of our men we are extremely well qualified to do the job. This afternoon I was pleased to hear from all sides of the House confirmation of the capability of the Canadian Armed Forces in this respect. Perhaps some hon. members may not realize that starting with the Chief of the Defence Staff, General Dextraze, many of the officers who are today planning Canada's participation in the Middle East have themselves taken part in peacekeeping operations around the world, including the Middle East itself.
Some 29 years ago General Dextraze, as a Lieutenant-Colonel, served under the United Nations in Korea. Ten years ago, as a Brigadier General, he was the first Canadian officer named as Chief of Staff of all the United Nations peacekeeping forces in the Congo. In this respect I am certain that the House will also be interested to know, and in fact be re-assured to know, that the officer we have selected to command the Canadian contingent in this most recent peacekeeping endeavour, Brigadier General Nicholson, was himself, as a major, stationed in the Sinai Peninsula 17 years ago in 1956.
I mention only these two officers by name to indicate in part the depth of our experience, but hundreds, and in fact thousands, of personnel in the Canadian Armed Forces have taken part in peacekeeping operations around the world. And now, Mr. Speaker, once again personnel from the Canadian Armed Forces are leaving Canada, not to fight but to prevent fighting. They are leaving for the Middle East, taking with them their experience and their dedication. They go in peace. Above all, they go with our best hopes for the success of their mission, a mission that is bound to be unforgettable and meaningful to each one of them as an individual, a mission that I believe is of importance to Canada, and a mission that can be of lasting significance to the achievement of peace in the world.

ments in a war in which they say they have no interest. The latest figures released in connection with the 17-day war indicate that some 1,800 of those killed were in the Israeli army. Let me give hon. members an idea of what that means in terms of population. It would mean that
16,000	Canadians were killed. It would mean 108,000 men as far as the United States is concerned. That is how serious the position is. I suggest to the minister that when he gets over there to Moscow, instead of saying "Here's to you!", and "Here's to me!" he should tell them the time has come for them to realise that their conduct in the Middle East is detrimental to world peace.
What is the purpose behind the Soviet moves? Oil. We are all going to suffer because the Arab nations have struck at the industrial jugular of the western world and Japan by reducing the amount of oil they would ordinarily ship. How many people realise how powerful these Arab nations are? I went to the trouble to look up the production figures and, if the House will permit me, I shall place them on record. There is King Faisal of Saudi Arabia. I remember meeting him in San Francisco in 1945. He is king of a country which today produces 355 million tons of oil a year. The Amir Sabah as-Salim of Kuwait disposes of 137 million tons a year; the Shah of Iran, 289 million tons; Colonel Ghadafi of Libya, 109 million tons; President Boumedienne of Algeria, 51 million tons. Then, there is Shaikh Zaid of Abu Dhabi who caused the minister such difficulty when the hon. gentleman heard he had decided against sending any oil to Canada-that was the first time we had heard he existed! This country, Mr. Speaker, turns out 64 million tons of oil a year.
Here are some other rulers whose countries are rich in oil: Shaikh Khalifa of Qatar, 28 million tons; Sultan
November 14, 1973

Qaboos of Oman, 14 million tons; Shaikh Rashid of Dubai, 11 million tons. The total, Mr. Speaker, comes to 1,148 million tons of oil a year. And the U.S.S.R. is in there. That is what it wants. Unless there is a change in the attitude of the Arab nations, an attitude which presently constitutes almost a fatal thrust at the western world and Japan, the consequences are not hard to foresee.
What are the Arab nations using this power for? Blackmail. Any nation which does not fall into line with their views goes on the black list. While the Secretary of State for External Affairs, with the optimism which characterizes him at all times, has not told us the full facts in this connection. I think Canada will not receive more thanks from the Arab nations after the force goes over there than it did before the force arrived. Who is going to win the war in the Middle East? Who has won it? Not the combatants but the U.S.S.R. It has achieved that grasping control that it has been looking for for generations. When the minister talks to members of the Politburo next week, I hope he makes it very clear that Canada understands exactly what is taking place.
I do not read press dispatches often, Mr. Speaker, but I do recommend for reading an article entitled "Five minutes to midnight" by Joseph Alsop which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on November 8 last. He says:
One source of apprehension, it appears, is the tone the Kremlin has been taking with the U.S. government. Another source-and one by no means to be underrated-is the way the Soviet press has begun to talk about the Watergate horror as crippling to the President.
The article continues:
. .. the Soviets are already making conditional preparations to intervene with their own troops. In Egypt, for example, there is considerable evidence of the new presence of Soviet-made Scuds."
They are tanks. The article says they are still coming in.
This, Mr. Speaker, is how serious this matter is. No one need suggest to me that we do not have to have proved to us that a peacekeeping force is needed there. But with the Russians continuing to foment trouble and to throttle the western world industrially, that peacekeeping force has a responsibility that all of us can contemplate in face of a danger that I hope is not as overwhelming as it appears to be.
Egypt now says it will open the Suez canal. That is part of the aim of the U.S.S.R. Drew Middleton has stated that the reopening and improvement of the Suez canal, already under discussion in Cairo, would strengthen the Soviet Union's strategic position in the Persian Gulf and in the Indian Ocean. The only nation standing against this is Iran. Iran, the dominant military power in the Persian Gulf, is seriously concerned over the prospect of stronger Soviet forces in that area if the canal opens, says Drew Middleton.
I mention these things, without having a prepared speech, because I feel so aroused that the Canadian people do not realize today what is happening. They do not realize it in the United States because, after all, all they can say as far as Watergate is concerned is that no one has yet been drowned in Watergate. But other than that, what is happening in Washington has been to give to the
Middle East Peacekeeping Force U.S.S.R. the new hope and expectation of what it can get away with; it no longer fears the United States because it believes it is divided.
What about this force that is being sent, Mr. Speaker? The minister spoke with pride of Canada's reputation, and there is no disagreement with that. But I suggest to the minister that there must have been an awful lot of soul searching, because the government of Canada advised the number one combat force of paratroopers in Edmonton to get ready. Then, when I raised the question in the House, I attempted to move a motion under Standing Order 43 to this effect:
That this House views with concern the indecorous haste exhibited by the Canadian government in its anxiety to secure consent of objecting nations within the United Nations to having Canadians in the peacekeeping force for service in the Middle East, whereby without regard to the magnificent record of Canadians in two world wars Canada's No. 1 combat alert unit is to be placed in a secondary position in the peacekeeping force being given a responsibility-
-and I then used this phrase-
-analogous to that of hewers of wood and drawers of water-
Then, the government backed up and did the proper thing. It decided to mobilize the Signals from Kingston. I see the minister smile, as if that were one of his contributions. But let me say this to him. The government turned a complete somersault.

Mr. Speaker, the House has been very considerate and I have tried, with whatever capacity I have, to warn this government and the people of Canada that detente is only effective when both sides indulge in it. But when one side accepts it and implements it but the all-powerful U.S.S.R. gives it lip service, then it is as dangerous today as it was in the dark days of 1938 when I heard Churchill warn the British people, and they laughed at him, as when Eden gave the same warning and left the government. Today, we are in one of the most serious positions that the western world has been in during my lifetime.

Mr. Speaker, I was most interested in listening to the hon. member who has just spoken, because he is well experienced in both the external and domestic affairs of this country.
A year ago, now, I had the pleasure and the honour to accept an invitation from the government of Israel to visit
26635-63;

Middle East Peacekeeping Force that country, and before I go any further, I want you to know that I was impressed by how hard the Israelis are working so that their country will become a great country.
Unfortunately, in the last few months, war has erupted between Israel and the Arab countries, especially, the UAR and Syria. For our part, we, in the Canadian government, are not happy about this situation but we are among those who try to find a solution to the Middle East problem.
Today, it can be said that a modus vivendi has come about between the Arab and Israeli forces.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this modus vivendi will finally lead to a lasting peace in that part of the world. As a result of that difficult situation, Mr. Speaker, Canada, which is
6,000	miles from the Middle East, has despatched its soldiers. Why are they there? Not because they agree! We must consider several facts, Mr. Speaker. We have to ask ourselves if the Canadians who are over there agree with the Canadian position.
I think they do, because the members of our armed forces are anxious to restore peace. We are pleased to note that Canadians agree on that issue. How many Canadians endorse that principle? I have often spoken with my constituents, Mr. Speaker, and I don't know that many who would be interested in leaving tomorrow morning for the Middle East, Cyprus or Viet Nam. Dedicated people are needed for that, Mr. Speaker.
And are we dedicated? It is extremely important to bear that in mind. That dedication I think that we, the members of parliament, and the people of Canada must keep it alive. This is part, I would suggest, of the great Canadian dedication.
Today, Canadians are in the Middle East. Mr. Speaker, and I have talked about it to many people, we must show a lot of respect for those who agree to leave for the Middle East.
